abstract: Automated fact-checking tools, cheap and fast but imperfect, are increasingly available on social platforms. We study when such tools can backfire in a sequential social learning model of misinformation. Agents observe an article’s reliability and their predecessors’ actions, which indicate whether they liked or disliked the article. They may also pay to fact-check it. We examine how welfare, defined as the probability of a correct cascade, changes when a free, error-prone automated tool supplements costly but perfectly accurate manual fact-checking. Two opposing effects arise. Broader use of fact-checking helps agents escape wrong cascades. At the same time, errors from the automated tool can mislead agents who would otherwise have verified the article perfectly, reducing the likelihood of correct cascades. We prove that adding the tool strictly lowers welfare for articles of intermediate reliability when truthful articles are not too informative and manual checking is sufficiently costly. Simulations show that the tool can help on either side of the intermediate range, and that it improves on manual-only checking on average only above a threshold accuracy.

sections.body: The paper asks when offering a free, error-prone automated fact-checking tool next to costly, error-free manual checking helps or hurts collective learning. Agents arrive in sequence, see an article's reliability and predecessors' like or dislike actions, and can fact-check privately, so a check reaches others only through the action it causes. The contributions are thresholds on reliability for correct and wrong cascades, a proof that adding the tool strictly lowers welfare for intermediate reliability under stated conditions, and simulations varying the tool's accuracy. The simulations show welfare exceeds the manual-only baseline only above a threshold accuracy.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Free, error-prone fact-checking tools can mislead others through actions, so their effect on collective learning depends on conditions.

sections.body: Each agent has a prior belief about the state, drawn from a continuous distribution, and sees the article's reliability, its message, and predecessors' actions. A fact-check returns a verdict with type-I error $e_{1}$ and type-II error $e_{2}$, and costs $K$. Agents update by Bayes' rule and check when the value of information exceeds the cost. Proposition 1 covers the case where the cost is below half of one minus $e_{1}$ minus $e_{2}$. Verdicts are assumed independent given veracity, and correlated or identical verdicts are left to future work.
sections.heading: The Model
sections.headline: Agents with heterogeneous priors observe article reliability and predecessors' actions, and may pay to fact-check before liking or disliking.

sections.body: Welfare is the probability of a correct cascade, and the change from adding the tool is the difference between the two method sets. Under Assumption 2, which makes the prior distribution symmetric and sets the shares of L and R fake articles equal to 0.5, the change splits into a term for truthful articles and a term for fake ones, weighted by reliability. The manual method has cost $K_{H}$ in $(0,0.5)$ and no error. The automated method has zero cost and error rates with $e_{1A}$ greater than $e_{2A}$, since automated checkers identify false claims more reliably. The asymmetric case is not analyzed.
sections.heading: Problem of Welfare Change
sections.headline: Welfare change decomposes into reliability-weighted changes for truthful and fake articles under symmetric assumptions.

sections.body: Three regimes depend on the manual cost and the automated accuracy, and regime (iii), where only the automated method is used, is the main case. Simulations set the automated error rates to 0.3 and 0.1, the manual cost to 0.3, and use a beta prior with parameters 0.5 and 0.5. Cascade frequencies come from 2000 runs on a 50 by 50 grid of reliability and p. Proposition 2 certifies signs only on some regions: truthful articles gain at some reliabilities and lose at others, and total welfare falls on an intermediate band when p is below a threshold. The two opposing effects are broader checking and misleading errors. Regime (ii) is treated only in an extension.
sections.heading: Simulations and Analysis
sections.headline: A proof certifies welfare loss for intermediate reliability when truthful articles are weakly informative, and simulations show gains elsewhere.

sections.body: The paper concludes that a free, error-prone tool helps by bringing more agents to check, but its errors, passed on through actions, can start wrong cascades that manual checking would have avoided. On average over articles, the tool raises welfare only when its accuracy exceeds a threshold, so the authors suggest platforms not offer it below that accuracy. The stated open questions are whether the threshold can be characterized analytically rather than by simulation, which operating point between the two error rates maximizes welfare for a tool of given ability, and which channels to offer when there are more than two with different costs and accuracies.
sections.heading: CONCLUSIONS
sections.headline: Automated tools raise average welfare only above a threshold accuracy, so platforms should not offer them before that point.

sections.body: The appendix derives the belief formula and the posterior odds update, the value of fact-checking with its cutoffs, and the proof of Theorem 1. The proof uses a likelihood ratio that is a supermartingale under a stated condition, Lemma B.1, and a lemma that a convergent limit must be stationary, Lemma B.2. Remark B.1 notes that the martingale property fails when $e_{2}=0$ over a range of values. The proof then covers cases (a), (b) and (c), using dominated convergence and symmetry between the two veracities.
sections.heading: APPENDIX
sections.headline: The appendix gives belief and checking-value derivations, cutoffs, and proofs of the cascade theorem and its lemmas.
